# Hardware plan for the smart irrigation system

Researched 2026-11-25 · 1 USD = 11 LYD · [العربية](HARDWARE_RESEARCH.ar.md)

Prices are planning numbers from public listings (marked listing) or estimates. Get local quotes on the exact part numbers before buying.

- Controller: **ET 200SP CPU 1512SP-1 PN** (S7-1500 family). OPC UA works in your TIA Portal V19 and PLCSIM Advanced simulates it, so the G5 tests carry over. For the bare minimum, the cheaper **S7-1200 1214C** also works with V19.
- Valves: **buried 24 VAC cable in the existing pipe trenches** (about 800 m on three runs). Every valve stays under the PLC's interlocks and nothing in the field needs batteries.
- Soil sensors: **wireless (LoRaWAN)**, 21 sensors at 12 stations and one gateway at the control room. No extra trenching.
- Head unit: a **speed drive on the booster**, an **electromagnetic flow meter**, a **pressure transmitter**, and a **level probe in the well** for steady pressure, water per zone, leak alarms and dry-run protection.
- Internet: Starlink is not available in Libya (talks on hold), so remote access uses a **4G router with an outdoor antenna**. Test Libyana and Almadar signal at the control room first.

Estimated total = Hardware + Freight + port tax 12% + Installation 15% (Lowest cost: 5%) + Contingency 10%.

- **Lowest cost:** The bare minimum with a used PLC, a spare laptop as the server, a consumer router, your existing pump starters and your own workers for trenching.
- **Bare minimum:** Only what is needed to run the 12 zones automatically and safely from the app.
- **Basic:** Minimum plus soil sensors, cheap fertigation and two cameras.
- **Recommended:** Industrial parts, wireless soil sensors, a pump drive and better protection.
- **Premium:** Everything, including solar pumping and per-zone pressure.

## Where everything goes

- **Control room:** PLC cabinet, 24 VAC transformer, UPS, surge protection, energy meters and pump drive inside; 4G router on the outside wall; LoRaWAN gateway mounted high on the roof or a mast; camera recorder.
- **Wellhead (just north of the control room):** Level probe hung in the well about 2 m above the pump intake, on its own cable. The pump protection relay sits in the control room.
- **Tank:** Hydrostatic level probe at the tank bottom, away from the inlet; cable out through the roof hatch.
- **Head unit at the booster pad:** In this order: tank outlet → booster pump (with drive) → check valve → fertigation injection → filter (clogging switch across it) → flow meter (straight pipe 5× diameter before, 3× after) → pressure transmitter → mainline.
- **At each zone valve:** Valve in a valve box at the zone's take-off from the trunk; solenoid wires joined with waterproof gel connectors; cable in conduit back along the trunk trench.
- **Soil sensor station in each zone:** Under a representative tree in the middle of the zone, away from the first and last rows, the valve end and the far end of the drip line; 20–30 cm from a dripper, inside the wet bulb. Mark the tree.
- **Around the farm:** Cameras on the control room, the head unit, the wellhead and the main track; solar panels on a ground frame near the control room.

Pipe routes on the farm map are a best guess, so cable lengths and valve spots are estimates until confirmed on site.

## When something goes down

| If this fails | What happens | How to override |
|---|---|---|
| Internet down | The app keeps working on the farm Wi-Fi and the schedules keep running on the farm server. Remote access returns with the internet. | Nothing to do. |
| Farm server or app down | The PLC keeps every safety interlock. In G5 the PLC also keeps a copy of today's program, so irrigation goes on. | Restart the server; meanwhile use the zone switches on the panel. |
| PLC down | Automatic irrigation stops; the pump protection relay still works. | Turn the pump and zone switches to Hand and watch the pressure gauge; or open valves by their manual screw. |
| Power cut | Pumps stop (no power to pump). With backup power the PLC and server stay on and show what happened; with solar the well pump runs by day. | Nothing to do; everything restarts by itself. |
| Valve coil or cable fault | The PLC sees no flow and raises an alarm for that zone. | Open or close that valve by its manual screw until it is fixed. |
| Sensor fault (flow, pressure, tank) | The app shows the fault and the PLC blocks automatic runs that depend on it. | Run zones in Hand on the panel while watching the pressure gauge, until the sensor is replaced. |
| Wireless box or radio down | Its valves close by themselves when their on-timer runs out. | Use the manual switch inside the box or the valve's manual screw. |

## Which controller

| Controller | OPC UA with your TIA V19 | PLCSIM Advanced | Price | Note |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| S7-1200 classic (CPU 1214C) | Yes | No | ≈ $650 + $100 license | Cheapest Siemens choice with OPC UA in V19; phased out from 1 Nov 2026. |
| S7-1200 G2 | Only from TIA V21 | No | ≈ $600–$860 | New generation; budget a TIA Portal upgrade. |
| ET 200SP CPU 1512SP-1 PN | Yes | Yes | ≈ $1,100 + $250 license | Recommended: matches G5 and your PLCSIM Advanced. |
| S7-1500 CPU 1511-1 PN | Yes | Yes | ≈ $1,000–$1,600 + $250 license | Most expandable; built-in display. |
| LOGO! 8.4 / Delta AS | No OPC UA (Modbus TCP) | No | ≈ $450 | Cheap, but needs a Modbus adapter in the app. |
| Unitronics UniStream | OPC UA built in | No | ≈ $900 | Includes a touch screen; programmed outside TIA. |

## How the valves are wired

| Option | Cost | For | Against | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Buried cable (recommended) | ≈ $2,000–$3,600 | Cheapest parts; no batteries; the PLC switches every valve, so interlocks always apply. | Trench work; long cables need surge protection. | Best for 12 valves within 300 m. |
| RS-485 remote I/O box | ≈ $600–$1,200 per box | Fewer long cables; easy to add southern zones later. | A powered box in the field to maintain. | Good if zones are added in the south. |
| Wireless valve controllers | ≈ $150–$385 per valve | No trenching; quick to install. | Batteries; valves outside the PLC's direct control; radio delays. | Use wireless for sensors, not valves. |
| Two-wire decoders | ≈ $150–$250 per decoder | One cable for all valves. | Needs the maker's controller; doesn't fit a PLC. | Not recommended here. |

## Buying and importing

- **Local (Tripoli, Misrata):** easiest warranty and support for Siemens parts and irrigation valves. Ask for quotes on the exact part numbers.
- **Import (Turkey, Tunisia, EU):** usually better prices for Siemens, Danfoss, Netafim and Bermad. Libya applies a 4% port services tax on the CIF value of most goods; sources disagree on further duties (0–25% by HS code), so confirm with a customs broker.
- **China direct:** good value for flow meters, generic transmitters and LoRaWAN sensors. Buy one sample first and check its documentation: Modbus register map, IP rating, cable length.

## Check on site before buying

- Pump nameplates: well pump and booster kW/HP, voltage, current; well depth and pump depth.
- Valve and pipe sizes at each zone's take-off.
- Real pipe routes (the map's routes are a best guess, and cable lengths follow them).
- 4G signal at the control room for Libyana and Almadar (a phone speed test is enough).
- The existing filter at the head unit and a spot for the fertilizer tank.
- The farm gate position (for a camera) and space for solar panels near the control room.

## Later additions

| Idea | Why | Rough cost |
|---|---|---|
| On-farm weather station | The farm's own rain and wind instead of a forecast grid point. | ≈ $700–$1,500 |
| Flow meter per zone | Exact water per zone, even with two zones running. | ≈ $150–$460 per zone |
| Pressure at the end of the drip lines | Confirms water reaches the last tree. | ≈ $150 per zone |
| Hosting with HTTPS | Needed for phone notifications on phones and safe outside access. | ≈ $5–$15 per month |
| Crop health maps (drone or satellite) | Spot stressed trees early. | Service |
| Standby pump | Automatic changeover if the well pump fails in summer. | Depends on pump |
